item.title: Does Saying Goodbye to a Pet Ever Get Easy?
item.description:
Grief

Does Saying Goodbye to a Pet Ever Get Easy?

As pets become family, letting them go gets harder.

Posted September 7, 2026

Key points
  • Veterinary medicine's progress has made end-of-life decisions harder, not easier.
  • Pets now hold emotional roles once reserved for people, deepening grief at their loss.
  • Love can cloud judgment: sometimes it means fighting on, sometimes it means letting go.

As a veterinary internist for more than 35 years, I have helped thousands of people make one of the hardest decisions they'll ever face: when to stop treating and let a beloved animal die.

Surprisingly, that decision has become more difficult.

Not because veterinary medicine has failed us. Quite the opposite. It has succeeded.

How the Human-Animal Bond Has Evolved

Forty years ago, the human-animal bond was there, but it didn't even have a name. Today, our pets sleep in our beds, accompany us on vacations, have insurance policies, and increasingly occupy a place in our emotional lives once reserved almost exclusively for other people.

Our world changed, too. We became busier, more isolated, less certain. In a chaotic world, our animals became a refuge. When I read the headlines, I hug our cat, Tommy. When I watch the evening news, I take our dogs Gracie and Eliza for a walk. Nothing seems to abate stress quite like burying one's face in a warm flank of fur.

I have known countless clients who sheepishly admitted that losing a pet was harder than losing a parent, sibling, or friend. They often feel guilty saying it. I understand why. Our animals share our homes, beds, and routines. We cook for them, talk to them, and worry about them. They don't judge us or hold grudges. Their love is pure love.

And we are responsible for them. Entirely.

That responsibility adds to the emotional decision-making. When I began practicing, there were things we simply could not do. Today, veterinary medicine offers CT scans, MRIs, sophisticated surgery, chemotherapy, and treatments for diseases that once meant certain death. There is enormous joy in being able to save a life. But every new possibility creates another question: How much longer should we keep going?

My Experiences With Christopher and Murphy

That question became personal for me with Christopher.

Christopher was my first dog, a magnificent Great Dane who weighed more than I did. He was silly, sweet, affectionate, and my shadow through veterinary school, internship, and residency. At 9, Christopher developed dilated cardiomyopathy. By 10, he had already exceeded his prognosis. Then one night, his stomach twisted. I knew immediately what had happened. Technically, Christopher had already lived longer than we had been given. But he had not exceeded "our" time together.

We operated.

I rationalized it. I told myself the surgery wouldn't be painful and that I would be there afterward for him to use my lap as a pillow. His heart was too sick. Despite everything we did, he deteriorated. He looked at me with those enormous brown eyes. He would fight as long as I asked him to fight. I had to be the one to tell him he didn't have to anymore.

With trembling hands and an agonized heart, I pushed the plunger until he relaxed into heaven.

I knew I had done the right thing. I also knew I had pushed too hard, perhaps six hours too long. Would I make the same decision today? Probably not. But I also know I could not not have tried.

Christopher taught me something I have carried throughout my career: Love, like tears, can cloud your judgment. Sometimes love makes us want to do everything. Sometimes love requires us to stop.

Years later, I had to relearn that lesson again with Murphy, a perfect Standard Poodle and my husband's first dog.

Murphy developed lymphoma. We agreed we would treat him as long as he tolerated chemotherapy and wasn't suffering. There would be no heroics. Eventually, my husband said enough. He was right. The day we euthanized Murphy, I vomited because I knew I had procrastinated. I had allowed my hope, and perhaps my profession, to get in the way of what I already knew.

That experience fundamentally changed how I practiced medicine. Unfortunately, it took me twice to learn the lesson.

How My Perspective on Treating Animals Changed

When I graduated, my job seemed simple: cure disease. Keep patients alive.

Somewhere along the way, I realized I had the wrong patient. I wasn't treating the dog or cat. I was treating the relationship between that animal and the person who loved them. My job wasn't simply to maximize the length of my patient's life. It was to maximize its quality and protect the bond that made that life meaningful.

I didn't want the cat spending its final days hiding under the bed because every interaction had become a battle over medication. I didn't want the dog undergoing procedure after procedure simply because there was one more test we could run. Most of all, I didn't want an owner looking back and saying, "I waited too long."

I have heard those words many times.

I have said them myself.

Guidance for Owners Facing End-of-Life Decisions

So what can I council?

First, don't wait for your pet to tell you they're ready. They may never tell you. Animals are remarkably stoic.

Second, pay attention to appetite. Most animals love to eat. When that changes significantly, pay attention.

Third, keep a quality-of-life calendar. Each night, give your pet a number from one to 10. Ten is a wonderful day. One is terrible. Write it down and watch the trend. It can give you some objectivity when your heart cannot.

Fourth, look into their eyes. Ask how they feel. Then be willing to hear the answer.

The hardest lesson is also the simplest: Don't wait too long.

We imagine death as a peaceful moment when an animal closes its eyes and drifts away. Sometimes it is. Often it isn't. There may be pain, anxiety, seizures, difficulty breathing, or other suffering. But we can make the end less frightening. We can ask for help. We can choose before a crisis makes the decision for us.

And then we can grieve.

How to Grieve and Honor the Bond

Our grief should never be guilt. It should be evidence of our love.

Our relationships with animals are worthy of mourning. They are worthy of remembrance. They are worthy of ritual. I have had the extraordinary privilege of seeing what animals do for us. They make us laugh. They comfort us. They give us routine and purpose. They sit beside us when we're sick. And they love us without asking us to become someone else first.

I spent my career caring for them. Now, as a playwright, I have begun trying to honor the bond itself. Perhaps that is the bargain we make when we bring an animal into our lives.

We agree to love them. We agree to care for them.

And eventually, we agree to let them go.

It is a terrible bargain.

It is also one I would make again and again.

item.title: The Search for Causation Comes from a Desire for Certainty
item.description:
Child Development

The Search for Causation Comes from a Desire for Certainty

Suggesting a singular cause for psychological challenges is reductionist.

Posted September 7, 2026

Key points
  • Headlines suggesting a "cause" for psychological challenges are reductionist and misleading.
  • It’s human nature to seek out certainty, causation and a "quick fix."
  • Adolescents deserve a holistic approach which considers biological, psychological, and environmental factors.

I’ve just read a headline suggesting that school absence causes obesity. Previous articles argue that childhood obesity is caused by poverty. Or poor parenting. Or the COVID pandemic. COVID has also been mooted as the cause of the apparent adolescent “mental health crisis,” and teen loneliness, and laziness, and “addiction” to smartphones.

Addiction to smartphones has been cited as the cause of pretty much all of society’s ills, even though smartphone addiction isn’t even a recognised diagnosis in adolescents.

I’ve been alerted to, and alarmed by, articles arguing that the “trend” in young people identifying as nonbinary or transgender is the effect of neurodivergence, or childhood trauma, or peer pressure—mostly via smartphones. There are claims that polyamory, asexuality, homosexuality, kink, and any sexual practice not defined as cis-het is “caused” by childhood trauma or abuse. Even though gender identity formation and sexual exploration are ordinary aspects of adolescent development.

Neurodivergence has been called a trend too, and its apparent cause is an overly lenient education system, or smartphone addiction, or poor parenting, depending on where you look. I’m not citing any of these nefarious causation claims because I don’t want you to google them and feed the algorithm.

The tendency to blame parents, usually mothers, for any physical or psychological challenge bequeathed to their children isn’t new. Original autism theories, dating back to the 1940s and '50s, suggested that children with autism had suffered a lack of maternal affection and been raised in "emotional refrigerators" akin to concentration camps. That might sound extreme, and I hope it does, but the legacy of those theories lives on in parents who feel blamed and shamed for their children’s diagnoses.

It’s human nature to seek out certainty and causation. People believe it will offer a “quick fix” to questions such as:

“Why can’t my child sit still?”

“Why is he overweight?”

“What caused the accident?”

“How did they die?”

“Why are they questioning their gender?”

“Who is to blame?”

Adolescents are not equations be solved
Source: Geralt on Pixabay / Free Download

I get it. Uncertainty and not-knowing are uncomfortable states. As a psychodynamic psychotherapist, I don’t offer quick fixes; I offer slow, thoughtful ones by helping people make sense of their feelings and experiences, and sometimes that includes making sense of their differences and diagnoses. I’m always curious about how they arrived at the here and now, and invite them to be curious too. We explore their personal and family histories, with a keen eye on themes that might link to whatever presenting issue brought them to my therapy room. But we’re not looking for a cause, or at least I’m not, because the human mind is not a computer programme or a maths problem; it’s way more complex than that. To suggest otherwise, to suggest there is one simple “cause” that created the “effect” would be reductionist, misleading and disrespectful to the multifaceted human who sits before me.

The adolescents and young adults I work with deserve a more holistic approach which considers biological, psychological and environmental factors. I’m curious about their development, physical health and genetic history (the biological stuff). I’m interested in where and how and who they live with, their family, peer and sexual relationships, their support systems and significant life events. And I’m curious about any trauma or adversity and the strategies they employed to manage them (the psychological and social stuff).

Adolescents and young adults are not equations to be solved. Their challenges don't have a singular cause. Lack of curiosity leads to ignorance, blame, shame, and stigma. That’s the only cause-and-effect equation I’m sure of.

item.title: Why the TV Series Sterling Point Feels So Precisely Gen Z
item.description:
Media

Why the TV Series Sterling Point Feels So Precisely Gen Z

Five ways a TV series nails how this generation thinks about love and family.

Posted September 7, 2026

Key points
  • Prime Video’s new young-adult series Sterling Point has gone viral for its sharp, witty portrayal of Gen Z.
  • The series captures a generation fluent in attachment styles, trauma, boundaries, and therapy-talk.
  • Sterling Point explores how family secrets, adoption, and sibling bonds affect identity.
Sterling Point
Source: Barry King / Alamy

Spoiler Alert: The discussion includes spoilers about the characters and relationships featured in the series Sterling Point.

Prime Video’s Sterling Point has many of the ingredients of an irresistible coming-of-age drama. It has an idyllic summer setting, complicated families, messy romantic choices, and enough buried secrets to ensure nobody can sit by the lake and enjoy themselves.

Created by Megan Park, the series follows 17-year-old Annie Jacobson (Ella Rubin), who discovers that she and her twin brother Connor (Keen Ruffalo) have inherited a remote Canadian island from the grandfather they were never allowed to meet. What begins as Annie’s attempt to uncover her family history quickly turns into a story about adoption, identity, and siblinghood,

Five things Sterling Point gets especially right:

1. Gen Z Is Fluent in Mental Health Lingo

One of the funniest running jokes in Sterling Point belongs to Maple (Mabel Strachan), Oona’s precocious younger sister, who appears to be pursuing an unsupervised graduate degree in psychology. Her reading material includes Bessel van der Kolk’s The Body Keeps the Score, Alice Miller’s The Drama of the Gifted Child, and Mel Robbins’ The Let Them Theory.

When Maple is asked about The Body Keeps the Score, she explains that she needs to find out exactly what the score is and where in the body it is being kept.

She is a child taking the title of an enormously influential trauma book hilariously literally. I’m not entirely convinced that a child dealing with her mother’s absence needs to be casually working her way through the trauma canon; seeing these books showcased in the first place is striking.

Psychological ideas that were once largely confined to therapy offices, graduate programs, and clinical textbooks now circulate through social media, podcasts, bestselling books, television, and ordinary conversation.

Connor barely hesitates after hearing about Oona’s romantic history before wondering whether she might be avoidantly attached. Apparently, for Gen Z, “What’s your attachment style?” is just as basic as “What do you do?” And “Where are you from?” when getting to know someone.

This increased psychological literacy can add value. Learning about emotional neglect, for example, helps a person see that meeting material needs does not mean emotional needs were met. However, acquiring psychological vocabulary doesn't bring emotional immunity or healing.

2. The Family Secret Is Rarely Secret From the Family

Annie and her twin brother Connor were adopted and raised in New York by their father, Steven (Jay Duplass). Then she meets Ramona (Amélie Hoeferle), the sister she never knew existed.

Families may believe that keeping secrets protects the family system. Adults convince themselves that children are too young to understand, that certain information would only hurt them, or that an event from years ago is better left buried (Minuchin, 1984).

However, children are often excellent emotional detectives. They may not know what happened, but they notice the subject that makes everyone suddenly weird or the name everyone avoids. They see an innocent question produces a wildly disproportionate reaction. They see when pieces of the family story don't fit. Kids aren’t as gullible or oblivious as we like to think.

Family secrets can create two contradicting realities: the official story and the emotions surrounding it.

When the truth finally emerges, the rupture isn't even about the reveal. It’s about discovering that people they trusted knew something fundamental about their lives and decided to keep it from them. That can be deeply destabilizing, creating mistrust and confusion.

3. Adoption Doesn't Require Choosing One Family Over Another

Annie’s desire to understand where she came from does not erase the bond she has with Steven, the father who raised her.

For some adopted individuals, questions about biological origins can become important parts of identity development. There may be curiosity about physical resemblance, temperament, family history, culture, medical history, or the circumstances that led to the adoption.

Adopted people can sometimes feel pressure, implicitly or explicitly, to demonstrate gratitude or loyalty by not asking too many questions about their origins. But wanting to know where you came from and knowing where you belong can coexist (Kennedy, 2022).

4. DNA Can Make You Sisters, It Can't Give You a Shared Childhood

The relationship between Annie and Ramona is one of the most interesting in the series precisely because their biological connection exists before their emotional relationship does.

They are sisters, but they are also strangers.

Sibling intimacy is usually built through thousands of ordinary experiences: sharing bedrooms and bathrooms, fighting in the back seat, knowing which parent is more likely to say yes, stealing clothes, remembering each other’s humiliating experiences, holding completely unreasonable grudges, and sharing elaborate inside jokes that no one else could get (Balan, 2023).

Annie already has that history with Connor. Their twinhood is complicated, but it’s not just a biological fact. They share references, memories, rhythms, and stories carried through an entire childhood. When Annie’s understanding of their family begins to unravel, Connor, even though he mostly annoys her, is one of the constants she falls back on.

Ramona cannot instantly occupy that kind of space simply because they share DNA. Annie and Ramona have to build a sibling relationship from scratch, which siblings don’t have to do. The awkwardness in their connection feels realistic, since biology may explain why someone looks familiar, but it cannot manufacture intimacy.

5. Self-Awareness Doesn't Make You Less Messy

The characters of Sterling Point recognize attachment patterns while getting tangled in their own. They understand that their parents are flawed and are still furious about the ways those flaws affected them. Even though they can explain why someone behaves the way they do, it doesn’t change the pain those dynamics evoke.

Insight is helpful, but it doesn’t magically fix things. One of my favorite parts of this show—despite the book selection—is how the characters use humor to survive.

The writing is quick, self-aware, and extremely witty, which keeps the series’ psychological language from becoming heavy-handed. That balance of sarcasm, wit, and psychological literacy may be one of the more accurate portraits of this generation.

In my own practice, I work with many young adults from this generation, and I am often struck by how well-versed they are in psychology. They know the language of attachment, trauma, boundaries, and family dynamics, and they have an extraordinary sense of humor. Metaphor, satire, sarcasm, and the occasional perfectly timed dark joke are gateways for talking about experiences that are otherwise difficult to put into words.

They may know exactly why they do what they do and have a very funny meme explaining it. We may repeat our patterns of behavior even when we know the language for our patterns. Sterling Point shows that self-awareness may have changed the way this generation talks about growing up, but growing up is still complicated.

item.title: How to Argue and Win
item.description:
Workplace Dynamics

How to Argue and Win

How to disagree and preserve the relationship.

Posted September 7, 2026

Key points
  • A careful choice of words is needed to successfully disagree with someone.
  • Arguing effectively, particularly when the other person is about to make a mistake, is critical.
  • The best teams and relationships are those where disagreement is safe when expressed respectfully.

This post was coauthored by Scott Allen and Ron Riggio.

Imagine your boss (or a colleague or loved one) is about to embark on a plan that you are sure will lead to disaster. Despite your misgivings, your boss is going full speed ahead. What do you do? Do you stay silent and let the flawed decision move forward, or do you speak up, state your disagreement, and run the risk of damaging your relationship and looking like you aren’t a team player?

The key is to learn the skills of how to disagree successfully.

Here are seven strategies for successful disagreeing that can help avert disaster and save your relationship.

  1. Use "I" statements: Frame the pushback as your own perspective rather than a correction of theirs. This keeps the conversation from feeling like an accusation. Try: "I think another perspective worth considering is..."
  2. Acknowledge their point of view first: Validate what's strong about their idea or decision before you add your own view. People listen differently once they feel heard. Try: "I think that's a strong starting point, and I'd add..."
  3. Ask clarifying questions: A well-placed question invites the other person to think out loud and signals that you're engaged, not resistant. Try: "Can you walk me through how this approach addresses [X] concern?"
  4. Bring data and facts: Grounding the conversation in evidence keeps it about the issue instead of about who's right. Having data to back up your argument definitely helps. Try: "The numbers we have show a different approach could improve efficiency by 15 percent."
  5. Suggest an alternative: Opposing an idea puts people on the defensive. Proposing an alternative gives them something to build on instead. Try: "Would it make sense to pilot this on a smaller scale before we commit fully?"
  6. Keep your tone neutral: The words matter less than the delivery. A calm, even tone signals confidence and respect at the same time. Try: "That approach makes sense to me, and I'd also suggest we look at..."
  7. Name the shared goal: Reminding the group of what everyone actually wants turns a disagreement into a shared problem to solve. Try: "I think we're both trying to get to the same outcome. Here's an option that might get us both the win..."

Here are some other ways to bring successful disagreement to the conversation:

  • "I think that's a strong idea, and I'd add..."
  • "That's one option; another consideration may be to..."
  • "Here's another angle: What if we added X and Y to the plan?"
  • "I like the spirit of that idea, and I am wondering how that may be received by [insert audience]?"
  • "What would [insert name] say from a tactical point of view?"

None of these techniques ask you to soften your view or shrink in the moment. They ask you to deliver the message in a way someone can actually receive it. They help you show up as an active, engaged participant. That distinction is the core of this successful arguing skill.

The best teams and relationships are those where disagreement is safe enough to be expressed respectfully and out loud.

item.title: Creating a Satisfying Retirement Experience
item.description:
Aging

Creating a Satisfying Retirement Experience

How do we navigate the joys and challenges of the retirement process?

Posted September 7, 2026

Key points
  • Retirement can offer an opportunity to step away from the “tyranny of the should.”
  • As we rebuild our futures, acknowledging our vulnerabilities can help us find our new place in the world.
  • Sharing our stories can help us connect with others and make sense of where we are and where we want to go.

My sister is turning 66. As she begins to contemplate retirement, she is thinking about her hopes and dreams for this next stage of her life. We recently had an extensive conversation about her anticipated income and her plans for retirement. Like many of her contemporaries, she hopes to travel, spend time with family and friends, work on a few creative projects, increase her physical activity, and slow down the pace of her days. As we discussed her circumstances, it became evident that her hopes for this next stage of life are overshadowed by concerns about her finances. After considerable discussion and thought, she has decided that, mainly for financial reasons, she will have to postpone retirement. My sister’s situation is not unusual. For many older adults, particularly women, the decision to retire is shaped by economic circumstances. The well-known image of retirement as a time of freedom, travel, leisure, and self-discovery can erode in the face of uncertain health and financial insecurity.

Navigating the Challenges of Retirement

I have also recently retired from full-time work. I am grateful that the nature of my profession allows me to continue to work on a part-time basis. At the same time, I recognize that some of the work I enjoy and find satisfying may not be sustainable for a prolonged period. The fear that I will become irrelevant, that my expertise will be perceived as dated, and that invitations for work will dry up has made the work I am able to do more precious; it has also made me feel vulnerable and anxious. For 30 years, I have studied, researched, taught, written, and spoken about well-being in later life. I am familiar with research on the joys and challenges of aging. I know that we are living longer, healthier, and fulfilling lives. But regardless of what we do, at some point we all have health concerns, experience loss and bereavement, will provide and need care, and might feel lonely and isolated. As we navigate these challenges, we also have to manage the vulnerability and fragility that emerges from knowing that the information, skills, and competence that we have worked hard to establish may erode, and that we may lose our hard-earned place in the world. We may fear becoming invisible or silenced, a phenomenon that many aging adults experience, particularly aging women.

Studies suggest that retirement brings a sense of relief and freedom—release from some of the obligations and expectations that have structured our lives. Retirement can offer an opportunity to step away from what Karen Horney (1950), exploring women's social expectations, described as the “tyranny of the should.” At the same time, we also lose meaningful work that provides income and structures time, creates relationships, provides recognition, confers status, gives purpose, establishes identity, and maintains a sense of being needed.

Words of Wisdom From Life Story Project Participants

I have had extensive conversations with a diverse group of older adults who have been a part of an ongoing community project on well-being in later life. The project has been a part of a "Livable Communities Consortium" sponsored by the World Health Organization and AARP. I started “The Life Story Project” in 2013. Over the years, more than 100 older men and women have shared their life journeys with us. More than 80 percent of those who participated in the project have now retired. With permission, I have written about some of the experiences that they shared during individual and group conversations and interviews. We have talked about their challenges, the joys they have experienced, and the unexpected realities they have faced. Below are three points that summarize their words of wisdom.

  1. Coping with an ordinary day: The unexpected importance of everyday. Often when we prepare for retirement, like my sister, we tend to think about the big questions: Will we have enough money? Where will I live? Will my health hold up? Will I be able to travel? What will I do with all that free time? But retirement is lived one day at a time. And it may be the ordinary Wednesday that becomes the challenge. Without the external rhythms imposed by work, one day can easily flow into another. The weekend no longer has the same meaning. Adjustment necessitates a redefinition of daily routines. Suddenly, those activities that we rushed through, often mindlessly—baths, breakfast, meal preparation, exercise, house management—no longer need to be rushed; they can become meaningful in themselves. Slow and mindful daily rituals—a walk, a conversation over tea or coffee, and listening to or creating music or making art can make the ordinary day more meaningful and fulfilling.
  2. Managing fragility and vulnerability: Adjusting to any new stage of life involves recognizing the range of feelings we are experiencing—feeling gratitude but also giving ourselves permission to grieve about what we have left behind. Neimeyer’s (2001) Meaning Reconstruction Model suggests that coping with any major life changes involves two steps: acknowledging our feelings, both positive and negative, and constructing a satisfying new reality, one day at a time. This process is not linear; it can take time. We may move back and forth between grieving what we have lost and discovering new things that bring us meaning, pleasure, and a sense of purpose. Looking forward to something new, returning to activities we have enjoyed in our past, or developing creative outlets can all help us build a satisfying retirement.
  3. Sharing our stories and connecting with others in similar circumstances: Sharing our stories is a powerful way to manage our new reality and connect with others. Our narratives allow us to reflect on where we have been and make sense of where we are and where we want to go. We can share what we are grateful for and what has changed, and begin to create a new understanding of who we are now. Sharing stories can be particularly helpful in giving voice to those who feel silenced or invisible. Stories can also provide us with legacy. They can help us connect across the generations, share our experiences, and reconstruct our sense of meaning and purpose. Stories can help us answer questions about life after retirement. Who am I now? What do I contribute? Who needs me? What makes my day meaningful and enjoyable? Where do I belong? What is my place in the world? In telling our stories, we can let go of parts of our past and at the same time build a more meaningful life story for this next chapter of our lives.

Retirement is not life’s sunset; it is one of life’s many stages. According to studies, retirement stages range from the initial “honeymoon” in the first year to a period of “disenchantment,” followed by “reorientation” and, eventually, stability and acceptance. This understanding of retirement reminds us that retirement is a process and that adjustment takes time. As we live longer lives, the concept of retirement has also changed dramatically. Like other stages of life, retirement has become more flexible and fluid. People move in and out of paid employment, work part-time, consult, build businesses, volunteer, teach, create, and develop a new “chosen” path.

item.title: Don't Let Denial Destroy You
item.description:
Denial

Don't Let Denial Destroy You

Personal Perspective: How denial may have cost my mother her life.

Posted September 7, 2026

Key points
  • Denial can be a helpful defense but it can also be life-threatening.
  • The cost of denial on interpersonal relationships is steep.
  • When a loved one is in denial, we can help them through acts of loving kindness.
Source: Tracy Strauss

To be dogged or not? To what end is the question.

On Labor Day 2011, my mother died from the doggedness of ovarian cancer.

All her life, my mother was dogged about maintaining her good health, so the news of her Stage IIIC ovarian cancer diagnosis at the age of 65 was a shock—but not really. My mother’s older sister had died of ovarian cancer, which prompted my mother to go for additional yearly screenings for the disease known as “the silent killer.”

Six months before her cancer diagnosis, a routine pelvic exam and ultrasound showed a “white spot” in my mother’s uterus. My mother’s doctor promptly recommended an MRI. But my mother refused, explaining she wouldn’t be able to go through with the procedure, because the tube she'd have to lie in would make her feel as if she were “in a coffin.”

Denial As a Defense

My mother’s fear was dogged. So was her denial. According to The National Library of Medicine, denial can be a helpful defense for cancer patients, but it can also be dysfunctional, and life-threatening.

Many months after the ultrasound, my mother began to experience ovarian cancer symptoms. Soon, she would find out that the “white spot” was a malignancy, which spread into her lymph nodes and abdomen.

In the hospital post-surgery, my mother asked me to log in to her work email account so that I could respond to any pressing emails for her without anyone finding out she was sick.

For the next year, my mother passed off her work absences as “a stomach issue.” To her co-workers, she introduced her cancer wig as “a new hairstyle,” for which she received many compliments. Even after the chemo treatments ended and my mother’s thick curly hair regrew, she continued wearing the wig to work. When she died and I informed her boss and colleagues that my mother would not be coming back to the office, they were in disbelief.

My mother doggedly kept up appearances. Her worst fear was the truth. Her dogged denial had great consequences.

The Cost of Denial

When I was diagnosed with complex PTSD in 2003 and disclosed to my mother that my father had sexually abused me when I was growing up, my mother said, “I know it happened, there were signs.” And yet at the same time, during all those years of my childhood, she'd turned her back on what was happening in our house, including the spousal abuse she was suffering. In 2003, she explained that if she’d faced what was happening to me then she “wouldn’t be able to function.”

According to renowned trauma expert and psychiatrist Dr. Judith Herman, in her book Trauma and Recovery, “the ordinary response to atrocities is to banish them from consciousness. Certain violations of the social compact are too terrible to utter aloud: this is the meaning of the word unspeakable.”

Source: Tracy Strauss

A week before my mother’s death, I asked her if I could visit. She doggedly declined. “There’s no urgency,” she said over the phone. “I have a lot to do: shopping, cleaning, laundry.”

“I can help you with that,” I said.

My mother doggedly refused my help. “I can do it myself,” she said.

“Then I’ll just keep you company,” I said.

“We’re having a hurricane this weekend,” she said.

My mother and I had a complicated relationship, but my love for her was dogged, and I wasn’t going to let anything stop me from seeing her, especially as something deep within me was telling me there wasn’t much time left. “The storm isn’t until Sunday,” I said. “I’ll come on Friday.”

I spent the weekend with my mother, noticing her difficulty breathing in the morning and the way she waved me off when I asked if she was OK, her dogged insistence that she was fine and that I needed to go home before the hurricane hit. I told my mother I loved her. I told her I forgave her for not protecting me as a child. I hugged her goodbye. She told me she loved me, too.

I drove home in the middle of the hurricane, which had been downgraded to a tropical storm, my car hydroplaning on the highway. The rain came down in torrents and, as with intense grief, for a while I couldn’t see where I was going. The road appeared before me as a fuzzy wall of gray-white. Increasingly disoriented, I thought about pulling over but I was afraid that might be more of a hazard. I was determined to make it home safely, and somehow, four hours later, I did.

The Aftermath of Denial

Labor Day weekend, my mother checked herself into the emergency room, carrying a manila folder with her medical records, the whole truth of her cancer journey, facts she’d doggedly kept to herself. She'd refused to sign the HIPAA form to allow her doctors to speak with me about her condition or her prognosis. On Labor Day, my mother put down the exhaustive work of her denial. She told the nurse she knew it was the end, and then went into respiratory failure.

Throughout her crisis, my mother directed her doggedness toward what she thought was the road to survival, even as she knew—as I’d come to discover when I read the contents of the manila folder after her death—that her cancer was aggressive and terminal.

Source: Tracy Strauss

Anyone—and anything—can be dogged. But the question is, to what end?

Every Labor Day that I can remember, my mother doggedly cleaned out her walk-in closet, which always looked like a jungle. She’d spend hours going through her clothes, determined to accomplish her task, preening what no longer fit, making room for a new life.

We can doggedly wall off the truth, or the facts of our life, or our feelings, but all that does is create more suffering. Instead, we need to figure out what, and who, is more important, and put our attention there, because the obstacles that get in the way of our deepest connections, and a meaningful life, aren’t worth the cost.

item.title: "I Made a Mistake" Is Not "I Am a Mistake"
item.description:
Self-Talk

"I Made a Mistake" Is Not "I Am a Mistake"

The harsh inner voice you carry may have started long before you did.

Posted September 7, 2026

Key points
  • If you grew up emotionally neglected, you may be far harder on yourself than on anyone else.
  • A mistake stirs up a feeling, and a feeling you do not notice gains the power to hurt you.
  • You can learn to notice and name your feelings, and judge your actions instead of yourself.
Source: deagreez/AdobeStock

Marcus took the wrong exit on the way to dinner. "Of course I did," he muttered. "I can't even follow a map." He kept replaying that in his head for the entire drive, 10 minutes late and furious at himself, while his wife sat quietly beside him, wondering what she had done wrong to make him so angry.

Mia realized she had sent the client the wrong file. Her stomach dropped. "How did I let that happen?" she thought. She quickly sent the right version, then sat at her desk ruminating about it, certain everyone would see right through her, and sure this was the moment they would finally realize she was not as capable as they thought.

Malik made an offhand comment that seemed to mildly offend his father-in-law. "Why did I have to say that," he kept asking himself. "I always seem to say the wrong thing." He felt his face go hot. "That's it. He's going to think I'm a jerk now. Twelve years of a good relationship now damaged, and this is what he'll remember. How do I always do this?" He couldn't stop attacking himself. He barely slept that night.

Do you see yourself in Marcus, Mia, or Malik?

Are you far more forgiving of other people's mistakes than your own?

When you make a small mistake, does it sometimes follow you around for hours, or even days?

If you answered yes to any of those, you are far from alone. As a psychologist who has specialized in childhood emotional neglect for years, I work with warm, capable people who are hard on themselves like this every day, and now I want to help you see how you may be getting in your own way. But don't worry, I am also going to tell you what to do about it.

The Feeling Underneath the Mistake

The clients I work with who are hardest on themselves almost all have one thing in common: they are not very aware of their own feelings.

Here's why. Every mistake, even a tiny one, stirs up a feeling. And a feeling you haven't noticed is far more powerful than one you have (Torre & Lieberman, 2018). It works on you invisibly, outside of your awareness, giving it extra influence over you.

Think of a pot left on the stove. Turn your attention to it, and you can lower the heat. Walk away, and it builds until it boils over.

That is what an unnoticed feeling does after a mistake. It hands your error far more power to hurt you than it ever should have. Marcus isn't really upset about the wrong exit. Malik isn't really losing sleep over one comment. It is the feeling underneath, the one they never stopped to notice.

Childhood Emotional Neglect

If you have never heard of childhood emotional neglect, you are in good company. It's one of the most common things I see, and also one of the most invisible.

Childhood emotional neglect is not about what your parents did to you. It is about what didn't happen for you. It happens when the people who raised you don't notice or respond enough to your feelings as you grow up. There is no single event to point to, nothing you would remember, no bruise and no bad memory. That is part of what makes it so easy to miss. It can happen in a perfectly nice home, with parents who love you and provide for you in every visible way.

But when your feelings go unnoticed year after year, you absorb a quiet message: that your feelings don't matter much, and neither, perhaps, do you. You also miss something every child needs to be given. You miss learning the emotion skills that carry you through adult life, like how to notice a feeling, name it, and manage it. No one sat with you and showed you how, so you grew up without those tools, managing as best you could.

Here's the part I most want you to know: many emotionally neglectful parents are doing their very best. Perhaps they were distracted, or struggling, or were raised in the very same way and never learned these skills themselves. They couldn't hand down what no one ever gave them. It's so often no one's fault.

And please know, the way you turn on yourself now is not your fault either. You were simply never taught any different. Once you really understand that, you can finally begin to stop blaming yourself for it.

What to Do Instead

The good news is that emotion skills can be learned at any age (Hodzic et al., 2018). The answer is not to stop making mistakes; no one can. The answer is to start noticing the feeling underneath, so it stops running the show. It happens in a few small steps.

  • Notice that you're having a feeling. When you make a mistake, and that familiar heat rises, take a moment to pause and register it. Say to yourself, "A feeling is happening in me right now."
  • Name it. Maybe it's embarrassment. Maybe it's the fear of being found out. Whatever it is, it is allowed. You may be surprised how much power a feeling loses the moment you accept it and put words to it (Torre & Lieberman, 2018).
  • Judge your actions, not yourself. There is a real difference between "I made a mistake" and "I am a mistake." Hold yourself accountable for what you did, and leave who you are out of it. The first one helps you do better next time; the second just wears you down (Singh & Bhushan, 2025).

Imagine Malik doing this. He still feels the heat rise. But this time he notices it, and he thinks, "I'm embarrassed, and that makes sense. It was a thoughtless thing to say, and I'll be more careful next time." Then he goes to bed. The mistake stays a mistake instead of becoming a judgment of who he is.

It Is Never Too Late

You were not born this hard on yourself. When your feelings go unnoticed, you don't learn to tend to them, and that's what happened to you. It's worth knowing, because what you didn't learn as a child, you can still learn now. I promise you that it's never too late. And the more you turn toward your feelings instead of attacking yourself for having them, the quieter that harsh voice will become.

© Jonice Webb, Ph.D.

item.title: Why You Keep Replaying Conversations in Your Head
item.description:
Default Mode Network

Why You Keep Replaying Conversations in Your Head

What overthinking says about your personality, and how to change the pattern.

Posted September 7, 2026

Key points
  • Replaying conversations is a sign of emotional sensitivity.
  • Rumination can feel productive but it actually amplifies distress.
  • You can learn to interrupt the replay loop, and it doesn't require positive thinking.

Julia, one of my clients, came to our last session feeling exhausted. She told me she didn't fall asleep until 2 am because she kept thinking about an interaction she'd had with a coworker the previous day. She was afraid she'd put her foot in her mouth, and the more she thought about it, the worse she felt.

Replaying conversations is incredibly common; I’ve heard stories like Julia’s from many clients over the years. They’re often frustrated because they know ruminating on the past negatively affects their mood. They can’t seem to step outside of the loop.

How your personality shapes overthinking

Neuroticism is a personality trait that describes how intensely and quickly you respond to stressors. This trait exists on a continuum. At one end, some people don’t get their feathers ruffled easily; at the other end, people are more emotionally sensitive. Most people sit somewhere in between.

At a basic, evolutionary level, emotional sensitivity keeps us safe by alerting us to danger. When a social interaction doesn't go the way we expected, we tend to focus our attention on the potential threat (the conversation) until we've figured out what went wrong. Repeatedly turning attention to your distress and its causes is called rumination.

Our brains aren’t always great at distinguishing between a real danger and a moment that just felt uncomfortable. And, as the dial on neuroticism goes up, our threat detector goes off more easily, making it more likely that we’ll ruminate following an awkward conversation.

Studies consistently demonstrate that rumination intensifies negative emotion rather than resolving it. Your goal may be to come up with a solution—thinking of something better to say next time or determining that what you said wasn’t that bad in the first place—but repeatedly turning the conversation over and over in your mind keeps your distress fresh.

If rumination makes us feel worse, why do we keep doing it?

Rumination can masquerade as problem-solving. When we turn a conversation over and over in our minds, it can feel like we're doing something productive. That sense of effort is enough to take the edge off the anxiety without taking steps that would resolve the issue or prevent similar events in the future, like apologizing or being more assertive.

Think of it like stress-cleaning when you should be working on a big project that’s due soon. You're busy, and you can pat yourself on the back for getting something done, even though the pressing task is still waiting.

The other reason rumination is so hard to break is a process called intermittent reinforcement. Every once in a while, replaying a conversation does lead to an ah-ha moment. You land on the right words for a follow-up, or you realize the other person was probably having a bad day and it wasn't about you at all. That occasional payoff is enough to keep you coming back to rumination as a coping strategy. Intermittent reinforcement means getting a reward only some of the time, and it’s one of the most powerful drivers of repeated behavior. It's the same mechanism behind slot machines; the next pull (or, in our case, thought loop) might be the jackpot.

What Changing the Pattern Looks Like

The good news is that the tendency to ruminate, and the neuroticism that underlies it, are not fixed. Personality traits are really just your characteristic patterns of thinking and behaving; and because those patterns are learned, they can be changed.

When people maintain new emotional responses over time, those responses become the new default. In practical terms, that means every time you choose to redirect your attention instead of ruminating, you are doing the work of lowering your neuroticism. The trait shifts because the behavior shifts, repeatedly, over time.

When you notice the replay starting, the goal is to turn your attention to what you need to be doing in the present moment. You don’t have to paint the conversation in a positive light or talk yourself out of caring about it. Just focus on your walk, your partner, or the work task you need to complete. The loop can't run when your mind is genuinely occupied with something else.

Each time you refocus, you have the opportunity to learn that failing to replay the conversation doesn’t lead to some unforeseen negative outcome. The next time the replay starts, the pull to engage with it will be a little weaker; you now have evidence that letting it go didn't lead to the disaster your brain was predicting.

The bottom line

Replaying conversations isn't a personal failing. It's what a nervous system wired for threat detection does when it can't tell the difference between danger and discomfort. The good news is that this wiring isn't permanent. Every time you choose to redirect instead of replay, you're changing it.

item.title: Ban on Students' AI Use and the Bigger Problem Facing Us All
item.description:
Artificial Intelligence

Ban on Students' AI Use and the Bigger Problem Facing Us All

Research shows disruptive innovations are declining. How can schools reverse it?

Posted September 7, 2026

Key points
  • To ban or not to ban: AI technology allows us to re-delegate what students will do mentally vs. externally.
  • To develop students' critical, creative, strategic, and ethical thinking, consider which tasks can use AI.
  • As knowledge expands beyond human limits, future innovators need to know how to use AI well.

New York City just hit pause on students' use of AI. Will other districts follow suit? And should they? The answer may impact all of us far into the future, as I explain below.

Perhaps we can all agree on the main question: What do we want to see in the next generation? Individually, productive citizens with fulfilling lives. Collectively, a better world than what we left them. But that is a tall order, as the world they inherit has huge, seemingly intractable problems like climate change. We expect them to tackle these problems with technology.

What Is Technology?

"Technology" is now synonymous with "computing." At one point, the wheel, pen, and paper were new technologies. Technology is simply an invention that expands our capacity to do things.

Writing as a technology overcame human limits on memory. Plato voiced reservations about moving from orality to literacy. The ability to recite at length was lost, rendered superfluous when everything was captured permanently on paper for perusal into posterity. The oral practice of preserving collective knowledge through dialogue morphed into manuscripts and libraries. In doing so, the collective minds of a Socratic circle multiplied a million-fold.

Internal Mental Resources vs. External Capacity

In placing the current debate on AI in context, consider what internal mental resources we want to preserve and nurture in our young. And what external tools and technology we want them to be equipped to use.

We want them to be able to think in ways that can stand up to the challenges that they will inevitably encounter. The key word is "think." Critical, creative, strategic, and ethical thinking are all essential in ensuring that the next generation can weather the storms to come—and thrive.

If we break each type of thinking into its task components, the question becomes clearer: Which part do we want our children to develop internally and which can we safely relegate to external supports?

For each type of thinking, a table below illustrates examples of tasks that may be relegated to AI or the student.

Critical thinking task components and example of AI use.
Source: Dysolve®

Critical Thinking

  • Skeptical examination of carefully selected valid information to arrive at sound judgment.

We could try to suppress students’ use of AI to do these tasks. Or we could allow them to do so but demand more. For example, ask them to justify why they picked certain options and discarded others.

Creative thinking task components and example of AI use.
Source: Dysolve®

Creative Thinking

  • Identifying problems, seeing new patterns, connecting disparate domains, and exploring solutions in situations with no right answers.

In a fluid, fast-changing environment, thinking outside the box is critical, as the world needs more inventors and problem-solvers.

Strategic thinking task components and example of AI use.
Source: Dysolve®

Strategic Thinking

  • Understanding the situation, identifying goals, crafting a feasible solution to achieve these goals, and anticipating opportunities and threats.

For workers, entrepreneurs, and corporations, strategic thinking is a survival skill.

Ethical thinking task components and example of AI use.
Source: Dysolve®

Ethical Thinking

  • Considerations of harm to others, society, and self.

Moral development should be embedded in our children's education, not just a course module.

The question in education is not just about AI use. The problem in education is in not getting students to practice all four thinking skills widely.

Where Were We Pre-AI?

Consider what the public school system was like before 2023, the watershed year for public use of AI. Poor literacy and math achievement was already endemic: barely one-third of students were proficient in national assessments (NAEP, 2023). Claims of causation demand valid evidence from causal studies. There are many possible culprits to rule out first: the pandemic, fewer families eating dinner together, less bedtime reading, the rise in children's screen time, and the rise in parents' screen time.

What Is AI?

Generative AI is not all there is to AI. AI is a collection of technologies that simulate human intelligence by performing tasks traditionally done by humans. Some forms of AI surpass human expertise in certain tasks due to the advantages of computing. By the same token, humans excel in other tasks over AI. So the trick is in getting the best of human ability and AI.

Challenge 1: 70% Not Proficient

The majority of students in the U.S. are not proficient in literacy and math. In this case, human capacity is simply insufficient to resolve the problem. Reading difficulty is primarily due to inefficiencies in processing language in the brain. This problem may require AI to overcome human limitations of capacity and speed (May & Van Horne, 2025).

Challenge 2: 30% Not Creative

Of the students who are proficient in reading and math, much is asked of them, given the societal problems they inherit. Humankind faces challenges that require big breakthroughs. We need disruptive innovators, yet they are less likely in the future (Park et al., 2023).

What Is Disruptive Innovation and Why Is It Declining?

As an inventor with software patents in AI, let me present it this way:

Criteria for different types of innovations.
Source: Dysolve®

An innovation has novelty. A patented invention is also non-obvious to even practitioners in that field. A disruptive innovation is novel, non-obvious, and revolutionary. Such breaks from the past combine disparate domains together in unexpected ways. This is creative thinking.

The exponential expansion of knowledge forces scientists to work in narrow slices, making potent connections across fields less likely. Schools need to train scientists-to-be to use technology to surmount this limit.

More than just rethinking AI use in school, we have to be willing to rethink education itself.

item.title: 4 Ways to Use Imagery to Become More Successful
item.description:
Imagination

4 Ways to Use Imagery to Become More Successful

We have an innate capacity to convey ideas and feelings through imagery.

Posted September 7, 2026

Key points
  • Quiet moments are opportunities to slow down and tune in to your inner wisdom.
  • Use the power of imagery to practice how you want an important event to play out.
  • A mental or physical health concern can be imagined as something you can mechanically control.
Source: Andreas Zeitler/Shutterstock

Before the development of language, our ancestors likely communicated and thought primarily through imagery and sensory experience. This may help explain why the mind remains so facile at using imagery as a way of representing and communicating ideas and feelings (Damasio, 1999; Kosslyn et al., 2006).

This post reviews four ways that you can use imagery to help yourself become more successful.

Quiet Your Mind

Have you ever had a great idea while you were walking outside? Or saying a prayer? Or taking a bath? Quiet moments are opportunities to slow down and tune in to your inner wisdom. Your subconscious does some of its best work when you’re relaxed and open to new ideas and suggestions. Take a little time every day to allow your mind to rest.

Here’s an exercise that can help: Imagine a sailboat at the lower tip of your breastbone. It floats there in that space. Now take deep, slow breaths. In your mind, watch the sailboat as it rises with each inhale and falls with each exhale. If you find your mind wandering during this exercise, calmly refocus on the sailboat.

Practice will make it easy to achieve the image of the boat and the calm feeling it gives you when you need it.

Change the Level

No matter the concern you are dealing with, imagine it as something you can mechanically control. You might do this by picturing a changing color, a sliding lever, or a dial you can turn up or down.

For example, you’ve probably heard the expression that someone is “seeing red” when they’re angry. Now imagine that anger is actually red. Next time you feel angry, close your eyes or put your hands over them and imagine that all you can see is red, Red, RED. Now choose a color for calm. Maybe an ocean blue?

Breathing slowly, focus on slowly changing the angry red you feel and see to purple and then to a calm blue. Or, imagine breathing in blue peace, and breathing out the red rage.

Even though this exercise is an act of your imagination, you will likely feel calmer after you make that color change, because you’ve given your brain a job to do and a way to ease an intense emotion.

Another example: Picture a dial you can turn up or down that represents your comfort level. Assign a value to each end (for example a dial set to “10” means you’re ready-to-scream stressed and a dial at “1” means you’re cool and calm). Now imagine reaching out and slowly turning that dial down.

Picture it moving, and imagine the stress being reduced in your body as the level decreases from 10 to 9 to 8 to 7 to 6 to 5 or lower. Imagine you are controlling it just like you would the volume on a radio.

See Your Success

Whether you’re planning to ace an exam, practicing for a big game, or prepping for an important conversation, use the power of imagery to practice how you want the event to play out.

Picture yourself studying, then confidently sitting for the exam and nailing it. Or picture yourself running that basketball play your coach wants you to work on, executing it perfectly not just once, but hundreds of times. Or picture yourself calmly explaining to a friend how something they’ve been saying to you is hurtful.

Using imagery to practice for an event can help move you toward the outcome you want.

Skip Forward in Time

One surprisingly powerful use of imagery is thinking of a future in which a problem you’re having has been resolved. This allows you to feel what it’ll be like to be free of a problem.

Sometimes, just considering that a source of fear or anxiety will resolve helps you feel hopeful. Plus, imagining a solution helps you explore which steps you can take now to get you to that future.

For example, sometimes you may feel pressure to excel in a particular class or activity. This can create a lot of anxiety, a feeling that doesn’t help. Now imagine yourself 10 years in the future, looking back on that challenge. What will you see and feel?

  • That maybe that pressured situation was not as do-or-die as it seemed in the moment?
  • That maybe you can approach this challenge the way you’ve successfully tackled something else?
  • That maybe you can accept one less letter grade in a class that’s a constant struggle, rather than expecting yourself to achieve at an “A” level all the time?
  • That maybe you eventually mastered the skill that’s been bothering you, so you can keep working at it with confidence?

Albert Einstein has been quoted as saying, “Your imagination is your preview to life’s coming attractions.” If you can imagine a future in which today’s challenges are things you accomplished or overcame, you’ll be on your way to making that your reality.

Takeaway

The methods described in this post represent simple ways to tap into our innate capacity for the use of imagery, which can help us think more clearly, feel calmer, and move toward the futures we imagine for ourselves.

This post is excerpted from my book, The Life Guide for Teens.
